mitigation: Use bounds-checked string/memory functions (strlcpy, snprintf with explicit size limits) throughout, and adopt a memory-safe language or a hardened C++ standard-library container usage pattern for new development where feasible.
Never pass user-controlled data directly as a printf-family format-string argument; always use a fixed format string with the user data passed as a data argument.
Enable and verify all available compiler/OS memory-protection mitigations (stack canaries, ASLR, DEP/NX, CFG) are active in release builds.
Integrate fuzzing into the regular development/CI pipeline (continuous fuzzing) rather than relying solely on periodic external VAPT engagements to catch this class of bug.

THICK-018.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. String-extraction and decompilation tools (strings, dnSpy/ILSpy for .NET, Ghidra/IDA for native code) and, if secrets appear encoded, a scripted approach to test common encodings (Base64, hex, simple XOR) against extracted candidates.
THICK-018.whatItIs: The compiled app itself contains hardcoded secrets — API keys, database passwords, internal service tokens, encryption keys, or cloud credentials — baked directly into the code or its resource files, instead of being loaded securely at runtime from a proper secrets vault.
THICK-018.rootCause: Developers put these credentials directly into the source code during development — often just for convenience, or because there wasn't a proper secrets-management system in place — and that habit carried straight through into the shipped product. Once an app is distributed to end users, anything embedded in it can be pulled out with basic, freely available tools — there's really no such thing as a 'private' secret inside a public binary.
THICK-018.impact: Extraction of any hardcoded credential grants the attacker whatever access that credential provides — direct database access, cloud infrastructure access, third-party API access, or the ability to impersonate the application to its own backend — often extending well beyond the local machine being tested, since the same hardcoded secret typically applies to every deployed copy of the application.
stepsToIdentify: Run a string-extraction pass across the full binary and all bundled resources, filtering for patterns resembling API keys, connection strings, JWT structures, or cloud-provider key formats (AWS AKIA-prefixed keys, etc.).

Decompile the application to trace any suspicious string constant back to its usage context, confirming whether it's actually used as a live credential versus an unrelated string that happens to match a pattern.
For candidates that appear encoded rather than plaintext, test straightforward decodings (Base64, hex) before concluding no secret is present.

Where a credential type is identifiable (a cloud API key, a third-party service token), attempt to validate it against that service's authentication endpoint (only with authorization, and using a read-only/benign check) to confirm it's live and current rather than a stale/revoked test value.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes extraction and, where applicable, use of any discovered hardcoded credential.
Extract candidate secrets via string extraction and decompilation as described above.
For each candidate confirmed to be a genuine, live credential, determine and document the exact scope of access it grants (which database, which cloud account/permissions, which third-party service).

Where authorized and safe to do so, perform a minimal, read-only validation of the credential's access scope (e.g. a benign authenticated API call) rather than a destructive or data-exfiltrating action.
Document every discovered secret, its type, its access scope, and whether it appears to be shared across all installations (versus somehow unique per customer/deployment).
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

variants: Hardcoded credential shared identically across every deployed instance of the application (highest severity, since one extraction compromises all customers) versus a credential unique to the specific tested installation.
Secret embedded in a bundled resource file (a config template, an installer script) rather than directly in the compiled binary itself.

mitigation: Remove all hardcoded secrets from source code and shipped binaries; supply credentials at runtime via a proper secrets-management solution (a vault service, environment-injected configuration) that isn't distributed to end users.

Where a client genuinely needs to call a backend service, use short-lived, narrowly-scoped tokens issued per-session/per-user rather than a single, long-lived, universally-shared credential embedded in the client.
Add automated secret-scanning (gitleaks, truffleHog, or equivalent) to the CI/CD pipeline to catch hardcoded secrets before they reach a release build.
Rotate any credential confirmed to have been exposed in a shipped binary immediately, since it must be treated as fully public once distributed.

THICK-019.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A fuzzing tool or manual test harness for whatever input surface is in scope (file import, form fields, command-line arguments, IPC messages), and a debugger to observe the application's behavior when malformed input is supplied.
THICK-019.whatItIs: The app accepts input — an imported file, a form field, a command-line argument, a message from another local process — without properly checking its type, length, format, or range before using it. Depending on how that unchecked input gets used later, this can cause anything from a crash to a logic error, unauthorized file access, or memory corruption.
THICK-019.rootCause: Input checking was either skipped entirely, or only applied to the 'normal' path through the app's own UI — while other ways of feeding the app input (directly editing a file, using command-line arguments, sending IPC messages) skip those same checks entirely. The assumption was that input would only ever arrive shaped exactly the way the UI itself produces it.
THICK-019.impact: Depending on where the unvalidated input flows, impact ranges from application instability/crashes (a low-severity denial of service) to path traversal (reading/writing files outside the intended directory), injection into a downstream interpreter (if the input reaches a command execution or query-construction point), or memory corruption in native code paths — the specific impact must be traced per input surface rather than assumed generically.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every input surface: file-import/open dialogs, form fields, command-line arguments, configuration file values, and any IPC/network messages the application consumes.

For each surface, test with boundary and malformed values: oversized strings, unexpected data types, path-traversal sequences (`../../`), null bytes, and format-breaking characters, observing for crashes or unexpected behavior.

Trace how each input flows through the application (does it become a file path, a database query fragment, a command argument, a memory buffer size) to understand what specific vulnerability class a validation gap would enable.

Cross-reference findings against more specific, related test cases (buffer overflow, deserialization, business-logic bypass) since a general input-validation gap is often the root enabler for those more specific, higher-severity findings.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes malformed-input testing against the test installation's various input surfaces.
For each surface, systematically supply boundary/malformed values and observe application behavior (crash, error, unexpected file access, or successful unintended action).
Where a path-traversal-shaped input is accepted, attempt to read/write a file outside the application's intended working directory as proof of concept.

Where the unvalidated input flows into a downstream interpreter/query, escalate testing toward the specific relevant finding (injection, deserialization) rather than treating this as a standalone terminal finding.
Document each vulnerable input surface, the specific malformed value that triggered unexpected behavior, and the resulting impact observed.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

mitigation: Apply strict, allowlist-based input validation (expected type, length, character set, range) at every input surface, not just the primary UI path, and validate consistently regardless of entry point (UI, CLI, file, IPC).
Reject invalid input outright with a clear error rather than attempting to sanitize/normalize it and proceed, which is a common source of validation-bypass bugs.

Apply the principle of defense in depth: validate at the point of input AND again at the point of use (e.g. before a file-system operation constructs a path from user input), since a single validation layer can be missed or bypassed.
Include boundary and malformed-input test cases in the standard QA/regression suite rather than relying solely on periodic VAPT engagements to surface these gaps.

THICK-020.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application, plus access to at least two versions of the application (a current version and a known-older, more vulnerable version) for the test machine you control. A network proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) capable of modifying the update-check/download response, and, where the update mechanism uses signed packages, tooling to inspect the signature-verification logic via decompilation.
THICK-020.whatItIs: The app's auto-update system doesn't stop you from installing an older version than what's currently running, or doesn't properly check that an update is both genuinely from the vendor and actually the latest one — not just an old version that used to be valid. This lets an attacker who can tamper with the update process force the app to reinstall a known-vulnerable older version, undoing whatever security fixes came after it.
THICK-020.rootCause: The update check confirms a package's signature is real — meaning the vendor did sign it at some point — but doesn't separately confirm the version isn't older than what's already installed. 'Genuinely signed by the vendor' and 'safe to install right now' are treated as the same thing, when they aren't — any version the vendor ever signed, including old, buggy ones, will always pass a signature check forever.
THICK-020.impact: An attacker positioned to intercept/modify the update channel (a network MITM position, or a compromised update-distribution mirror) can force a target client to downgrade to a specific older version chosen because it has a known, exploitable vulnerability — then chain that reintroduced vulnerability into a full compromise, effectively bypassing every security fix shipped since that older version.
stepsToIdentify: Obtain a genuinely-signed older version of the application (from the vendor's own historical release archive, if available) alongside the current version.
Proxy the update-check/download flow and attempt to substitute the older, validly-signed package in place of the current update response.
Observe whether the client accepts and installs the older package without any version-currency check, or whether it correctly detects and rejects the downgrade attempt.

Where the update mechanism relies on an update-manifest/metadata file separate from the package itself, check whether that manifest's own integrity/authenticity (and its stated version number) is independently verified, since manipulating the manifest alone (without needing a fake package) may be sufficient.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes update-mechanism manipulation testing against the test installation, and obtain a legitimately-signed older version with a documented, known vulnerability for use as the downgrade target.
Proxy the application's update-check request and substitute a response pointing to (or directly serve) the older, validly-signed package.
Trigger the client's update process and confirm whether the older version installs successfully.

If the downgrade succeeds, demonstrate exploitation of the specific known vulnerability present in that older version as the full impact chain, tying the update-mechanism weakness to a concrete, exploitable outcome.
Document the exact update-check/verification logic gap (missing version-currency check, unauthenticated manifest) and the specific downgrade-enabled vulnerability chained.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

variants: Unauthenticated update manifest, where only the package itself is signed but the manifest specifying which version/URL to fetch is not, allowing manifest tampering alone to redirect to an older package.

Signature check present and version-currency check present, but the version-comparison logic itself is flawed (e.g. simple string comparison rather than proper semantic version comparison, allowing a crafted version string to be misread as newer).

mitigation: Enforce a strict monotonic version check as part of update installation, independent of and in addition to signature verification — reject any package whose version is not strictly greater than the currently-installed version (absent an explicit, deliberate, separately-authorized downgrade flow).
Sign and independently verify the update manifest/metadata itself, not just the final package, so manifest tampering alone cannot redirect the client to an older or malicious package.

Maintain a server-side revocation list of known-vulnerable historical versions and have the client check against it (or rely on the monotonic-version enforcement above) so those versions can never be reinstalled even with a valid signature.
Use a well-tested semantic-version comparison library rather than custom string-comparison logic for the version-currency check.

THICK-021.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control, with standard (non-administrative) user access shared with (or accessible to) another local account for demonstrating cross-user visibility. Process Explorer/Task Manager (with the Command Line column enabled) or `wmic process get commandline` for process-list inspection.
THICK-021.whatItIs: The app (or a helper program it launches) passes a sensitive value — a password, an API token, a session secret — directly as a plain, visible command-line argument when starting another process, instead of using something more private like an environment variable or a temporary file. On most operating systems, any other user or process on the machine can see the full command line — arguments included — of anything currently running.
THICK-021.rootCause: Passing values as command-line arguments is the simplest way to hand data to a new process, and nobody weighed the sensitivity of that specific value against how visible command-line arguments actually are on the platform — they're treated as private, when in reality they're something any other local process can see just by listing what's running.
THICK-021.impact: Any other user logged into the same machine, or any lower-privileged process capable of enumerating running processes and their command lines, can read the exposed secret directly from the process list — without needing any special privilege beyond ordinary process-enumeration rights, which are available to standard users on most default OS configurations.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger the application to spawn the relevant child process/helper script (e.g. during login, an update check, or a specific feature invocation) while monitoring process creation with Process Monitor or Process Explorer.

Inspect the full command line of the spawned process (enabling the Command Line column in Process Explorer, or via `wmic process get commandline` / `ps aux` on Unix-like systems) for any sensitive-looking values.

From a second, separate local user account (or a low-privileged background process), confirm the same command-line argument is visible, demonstrating the cross-user/cross-process exposure rather than assuming it based on same-user observation alone.
Check whether the same secret is also exposed in shell history, system/application event logs, or process-accounting logs that record command lines.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes process-list inspection during normal application operation on the test installation.
Trigger the application action that spawns the process carrying the sensitive command-line argument.
From a second local user account (or a low-privileged monitoring process), enumerate running processes and extract the exposed secret from the command line.
Demonstrate use of the extracted secret (e.g. authenticate to the associated service/API) as proof of real-world impact, if safely and appropriately scoped to do so.
Document the exact process, argument, and the extraction method (which user/privilege level was sufficient to observe it).
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

Where feasible, have the child process retrieve the secret itself from a proper secret store rather than receiving it from the parent at all.
Audit all inter-process secret-passing mechanisms in the application for this pattern, since it's easy to overlook in helper scripts and updater/installer components specifically.

THICK-022.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A clipboard-monitoring utility or a simple script polling the OS clipboard API, run from a second application/process context to demonstrate cross-application visibility.
THICK-022.whatItIs: A 'copy to clipboard' button copies sensitive data — a password, an API key, a one-time code, a full card number — to the system clipboard, and never clears it afterward, and doesn't use any 'exclude from clipboard history' option the OS might offer. That means any other app on the machine that can read the clipboard can grab that secret for as long as it stays there.
THICK-022.rootCause: The clipboard is a shared, unauthenticated resource on basically every desktop and mobile OS — any app with basic clipboard access (which is usually unrestricted) can read whatever was last copied there. This convenience feature was built without accounting for that shared access, and without using the auto-clear or exclusion options meant to reduce exactly this risk.
THICK-022.impact: Any other application running on the same machine — including malware, a browser extension, or another user-installed program with clipboard access — can silently read the sensitive value while it remains on the clipboard, and on some platforms clipboard history features can persist the value even longer than the immediate copy operation, extending the exposure window further.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger the application's copy-to-clipboard feature for a sensitive value (a password reveal-and-copy button, an OTP code, a payment card number).
From a separate, independent application/process, poll the clipboard immediately after the copy operation and confirm the sensitive value is readable.

Measure how long the value remains on the clipboard before (if ever) the application clears it, and compare against reasonable practice (a short timeout, typically 30-60 seconds, is the common mitigation).

Check whether the platform's clipboard-history feature (Windows Clipboard History, for example) retains the value even after the application's own clear/timeout, and whether the application used the appropriate API flag to exclude itself from that history.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes clipboard-monitoring testing against the test installation.
Trigger the copy-to-clipboard action for a sensitive value within the application.
From a separate monitoring process/script, capture the clipboard content immediately and confirm the sensitive value is present.
If applicable, check the OS clipboard-history feature for continued presence of the value after the application's own session ends.
Document the exact sensitive data type exposed, the duration it remained accessible, and whether clipboard-history persistence extended that exposure.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

Sensitive value copied automatically (without explicit user action) as a side effect of another feature, increasing the chance of inadvertent exposure.

Minimize reliance on clipboard-based convenience features for highly sensitive values; where feasible, offer a masked, in-app "reveal" instead of a full clipboard copy.
Educate users, where the copy-to-clipboard feature is retained, that clipboard contents are shared system-wide and should be treated as temporarily exposed.

THICK-023.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application and its companion process(es)/service on a test machine you control, with standard (non-administrative) user access. Sysinternals Process Explorer/WinObj to enumerate named pipes/mailslots/shared memory objects, and their permissions, plus a means to construct and send arbitrary messages on the discovered channel.
THICK-023.whatItIs: Different parts of the app — the main window, a background service, a helper process — talk to each other over a local channel (a named pipe, shared memory, a local network socket) that either doesn't verify who's connecting to it at all, or has permissions loose enough that any regular local program can connect and send messages, not just the app's own components.
THICK-023.rootCause: These communication channels were built assuming only the app's own pieces would ever use them, without adding any access restriction (locking the channel down to the specific expected program) or authentication (a shared secret proving the sender is legitimate) to actually enforce that assumption.
THICK-023.impact: Any other local process — including malware or a lower-privileged process under attacker control — can connect to the IPC channel and either eavesdrop on sensitive data passing over it, or, more severely, send forged messages that the receiving (potentially more privileged) component acts upon, which can range from triggering unintended application behavior to a local privilege-escalation path if the receiving component runs elevated (overlaps with the improper-privilege-escalation finding for that specific escalation angle).
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the application's IPC surface: named pipes, mailslots, and shared-memory/mapped-file objects, using WinObj or a similar object-namespace browser (or `lsof`/`ls /tmp` equivalents for Unix domain sockets).
Check the DACL/permissions on each discovered IPC object for standard-user connect/write access using accesschk.
For channels found to be connectable by a standard user, capture legitimate traffic on the channel (where possible) to understand its message format.
Determine which component is on the receiving end of each channel and its privilege level, prioritizing channels feeding into an elevated process as higher severity.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes IPC-channel connection and message-injection testing against the test installation.
Connect to the identified IPC object as a standard user/independent process, confirming the connection succeeds without any authentication challenge.
Capture or infer the expected message format, then construct and send a forged message to the channel.
Observe the receiving component's behavior for evidence that the forged message was accepted and acted upon (a UI state change, a file written, a privileged action performed).
If the receiving component runs elevated, demonstrate the resulting privilege-escalation impact as the most severe evidence for the report.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

Connect to and send data on a discovered named pipe

variants: IPC channel feeding into an elevated (SYSTEM/root) receiving process, providing a local privilege-escalation path rather than just same-privilege message injection.
IPC channel carrying sensitive data readable by eavesdropping alone, without needing to inject forged messages at all.
Named pipe/IPC interception with weak ACLs allowing lower-privilege access
Memory scraping from accessible process dumps using volatility/WinDbg
mitigation: Restrict IPC object DACLs (named pipe/shared-memory permissions) to only the specific, expected process/service account, denying connect/write access to standard users or Everyone/Authenticated Users groups.

Authenticate the calling process at the application level in addition to OS-level object permissions — verify the sender's identity/integrity (e.g. via a signed message or a mutually-derived session token) rather than trusting any connection that reaches the channel.
Validate and sanity-check all messages received over IPC as untrusted input, regardless of the sending process's assumed identity.

Where the receiving component is privileged, apply the same least-privilege design principle as the general privilege-escalation findings: minimize what a single IPC message can cause the privileged component to do.

THICK-024.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A network intercepting proxy or packet capture tool (Wireshark, Burp Suite/mitmproxy) positioned to observe the application's network traffic to its backend.
THICK-024.whatItIs: The app talks to its server (or a local companion service) over a connection that's completely unencrypted (plain HTTP or a raw network connection with no TLS), or only partly encrypted — some features use HTTPS while others, like a telemetry check-in or license verification, don't. Whatever travels over that unencrypted part is visible to anyone watching the network.
THICK-024.rootCause: Not every feature that talks over the network got covered by the same 'always use encryption' standard applied to the app's main functionality. Secondary features — update checks, analytics, license pings — often get added later in development and slip past the security review that covered the primary traffic.
THICK-024.impact: An attacker positioned on the network path (a shared/public Wi-Fi network, a compromised router, or an on-path attacker via ARP spoofing on a local network) can passively capture and read the unencrypted traffic, and where it carries authentication credentials, session tokens, or sensitive business data, can achieve credential theft or session hijacking; where the unencrypted channel also lacks integrity protection, active tampering (response modification) is possible too.
stepsToIdentify: Capture the application's full network traffic during a comprehensive walkthrough of its features (login, primary functionality, settings, update check, any telemetry/analytics call) using Wireshark or a proxy configured to intercept all traffic, not just HTTP(S).
Filter the capture for any traffic on standard unencrypted ports (80, 23, a custom unencrypted port) or any TLS handshake that fails/downgrades unexpectedly.
For each unencrypted channel found, identify what data it carries — flag any credential, token, or sensitive business data specifically.
Cross-reference against the certificate-pinning finding, since a channel that does use TLS but without pinning is a related but distinct issue from one using no encryption at all.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes network traffic capture during a full feature walkthrough of the test installation.
Capture traffic across every feature of the application, including secondary/background channels (update checks, telemetry) not just the primary login/business-function flow.
Identify and extract any sensitive data (credentials, tokens, PII, business data) observed in cleartext.
Where credentials/tokens are captured, attempt to use them against the corresponding service as proof-of-impact evidence, using only test accounts.
Document every unencrypted channel found, the data it exposed, and its business purpose (primary function vs. a secondary/overlooked feature).
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

examplePayloads.command: tshark -i eth0 -w full_app_traffic.pcap  # perform login, core feature use, settings, update-check while capturing

Extract cleartext credentials from a captured HTTP POST

variants: Primary application functionality correctly using TLS while a secondary channel (telemetry, licensing check, crash reporting) uses plain HTTP.
TLS used but silently downgrading to plaintext on connection failure rather than failing closed, which an active attacker can force by blocking the TLS handshake.
Named pipe/IPC interception with weak ACLs allowing lower-privilege access
Memory scraping from accessible process dumps using volatility/WinDbg
mitigation: Enforce TLS for every network-communicating feature of the application, including secondary/background channels, with no plaintext fallback under any failure condition (fail closed, not open).
Apply certificate pinning (see the related finding) in addition to basic TLS to protect against a MITM presenting an otherwise-trusted certificate.
Conduct a full-traffic-capture review (as used in this identification process) as a standing pre-release check, specifically to catch overlooked secondary channels.
Disable or remove legacy, unencrypted protocol support entirely rather than leaving it available as a fallback.

THICK-025.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A disassembler/decompiler (Ghidra, IDA, dnSpy/ILSpy) and a debugger (x64dbg) to assess how readily the binary yields to standard static and dynamic analysis.
THICK-025.whatItIs: The app ships with no tamper protection, no code obfuscation, and no self-check for integrity at all. It's a straightforward build that decompiles almost back to readable source code, has nothing stopping a debugger from attaching to it, and never verifies its own code hasn't been modified while running or after installation.
THICK-025.rootCause: Binary protection just wasn't part of the release process — either the team didn't consider reverse-engineering resistance necessary for this particular product, or it was deprioritized in favor of shipping features faster. The result is a compiled app that's exactly as easy to analyze and modify as a raw development build.
THICK-025.impact: Full absence of binary protection significantly lowers the effort required for every other client-side attack documented in this domain (business-logic tampering, license bypass, hardcoded-secret extraction, hooking/injection) since none of them need to first defeat an anti-tampering layer — this finding is best understood as a force-multiplier for the other findings rather than a standalone, independently-exploitable issue.
stepsToIdentify: Attempt straightforward decompilation of the binary and assess how close the output is to readable, near-original source code (trivial for unobfuscated .NET/Java bytecode, more involved but still very feasible for unobfuscated native code).
Attempt to attach a standard debugger to a running instance and confirm no anti-debugging countermeasure triggers.
Check whether the binary performs any self-integrity check (a checksum/hash of its own code segments compared against an expected value) at startup, by searching decompiled code for such a routine.
Assess whether any commercial or open-source packer/obfuscator/protector is applied at all (even weak, defeatable protection is a materially different finding than none whatsoever).
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes static/dynamic analysis of the test installation's binary.
Decompile the binary and demonstrate the ease of obtaining readable logic for a security-sensitive routine (a license check, a crypto function) as evidence.
Attach a debugger and confirm unhindered ability to set breakpoints, step through execution, and modify memory/registers at will.

Where feasible within the engagement's scope, chain this finding into a concrete demonstration of one of the other client-side findings (a business-logic bypass or hooking demonstration) to show the practical consequence of the missing protection, rather than reporting it as a purely theoretical gap.

Recommend layered protection (commercial obfuscator/packer plus a genuine anti-tamper/self-integrity check) rather than relying on any single technique, since a determined attacker with static+dynamic analysis tooling can usually defeat one layer alone.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

examplePayloads.command: dnSpy target_app.exe  # or Ghidra for native binaries — check whether logic is fully readable without significant manual reconstruction

examplePayloads.label: Confirm unhindered debugger attachment
examplePayloads.command: x64dbg target_app.exe  # attach and set a breakpoint on a security-relevant function without any anti-debug trigger

examplePayloads.label: Search for (absence of) a self-integrity-check routine

variants: Complete absence of any protection versus weak/outdated protection (an old, publicly-defeated packer or an easily-bypassed anti-debug check) that provides negligible real-world resistance despite technically being present.

Anti-tamper checks (integrity self-verification, debugger detection) implemented but only client-side and easily patched out with a binary edit, versus checks that also report to a server-side verification endpoint the attacker cannot silence purely by modifying the local binary.
Named pipe/IPC interception with weak ACLs allowing lower-privilege access
Memory scraping from accessible process dumps using volatility/WinDbg
mitigation: Apply a reputable commercial or well-maintained open-source obfuscation/protection solution appropriate to the runtime, understanding this raises attacker effort rather than providing an absolute guarantee.
Implement runtime self-integrity verification (checksumming critical code segments at startup and periodically during execution) and anti-debugging countermeasures as defense in depth.
Prioritize moving genuinely security-critical logic server-side (see the client-side-trust-boundary finding) rather than relying on binary protection alone to safeguard client-resident logic.
Treat binary protection as one layer in a defense-in-depth strategy, not a substitute for proper server-side enforcement of anything with real security or financial consequence.

THICK-026.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A means to trigger an application crash (an invalid input, a debugger-forced exception) and access to wherever crash dumps or verbose logs are written (a local folder, or a remote crash-reporting/telemetry backend if the application uploads dumps automatically).
THICK-026.whatItIs: When the app crashes or writes detailed diagnostic logs, the resulting crash report or log file contains sensitive data that happened to be in memory or in the log context at that moment — passwords, session tokens, encryption keys, or confidential business data — because the logging or crash-reporting tool grabs a broad snapshot of everything without removing known-sensitive fields first.
THICK-026.rootCause: Crash reporting and detailed logging are designed to capture as much context as possible, since that's genuinely useful for debugging — but no step was added to strip out sensitive fields before that dump or log gets written to disk, or (in many products) automatically uploaded to the vendor's own crash-reporting service.
THICK-026.impact: Anyone with access to the crash dump/log file — another local user, a process with file-system read access, or, where dumps are auto-uploaded, anyone with access to the vendor's crash-reporting backend — can extract sensitive data that was never intended to be persisted or transmitted outside the running application's memory space.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger a crash or enable verbose logging while the application holds representative sensitive data in memory (logged in, mid-transaction) and inspect the resulting dump/log file directly for plaintext sensitive content.
Check whether crash dumps are automatically uploaded to a vendor backend, and if so, whether that upload occurs over an encrypted channel and to an access-controlled destination.

Review log-level configuration to determine whether verbose/debug logging (which is more likely to capture full request/response bodies including secrets) can be enabled in production, either by the user or by default.
Cross-reference with the general insecure-local-data-storage finding, since crash dumps/logs are a specific, commonly-overlooked storage location within that broader class.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes crash-inducing and log-inspection testing against the test installation.
Populate the application with representative sensitive test data (login, perform a sensitive transaction) then trigger a crash or enable verbose logging for the relevant operation.
Locate and inspect the resulting crash dump/log file for plaintext sensitive content.

If auto-upload to a vendor backend is confirmed, document the transmission channel's security (encrypted/unencrypted) as an additional exposure dimension, without needing direct access to the vendor's backend itself.
Document the exact sensitive data types found and the file's default access permissions/location.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

Sensitive data present in verbose/debug-level application logs even without any crash occurring at all.

mitigation: Implement redaction/scrubbing of known-sensitive fields (passwords, tokens, keys, PII patterns) before writing any crash dump or log entry.
Restrict crash-dump and log-file permissions to the owning user/administrators only, and apply the same access controls to any local staging location before upload.
Encrypt crash dumps/logs in transit if automatically uploaded to a vendor backend, and apply strict access control on that backend.
Default to a conservative (non-verbose) logging level in production builds, requiring an explicit, audited action to enable verbose logging temporarily for diagnostic purposes.

THICK-027.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control, with standard (non-administrative) user access sufficient to read the process's own memory, or administrative access if using a full memory-dumping tool. A memory-forensics tool (Process Hacker's memory-string search, WinDbg, or a dedicated tool like Mimikatz for credential-specific memory scraping where applicable) to search live process memory for sensitive content.
THICK-027.whatItIs: Sensitive data — passwords, decrypted tokens, encryption keys, confidential business data — stays sitting in the app's memory in plain, readable form for longer than it actually needs to, instead of being cleared right after use. In some cases this happens because the programming language's string type simply can't be reliably wiped from memory, even if the app tries to clear it. That means the data can be recovered later by inspecting the process's memory, or from a crash dump, well after it was actually needed.
THICK-027.rootCause: Sensitive values are often stored using the language's standard, unchangeable string type (like .NET's String or Python's str), which — once created — can't reliably be overwritten in memory before the system eventually cleans it up on its own schedule. Combined with no deliberate effort to clear genuinely sensitive values immediately after use, secrets end up lingering in memory far longer than they should.
THICK-027.impact: Anyone with the ability to read the application's process memory (a local attacker with sufficient privilege, malware running in the same context, or someone with access to a memory/crash dump of the process) can recover sensitive data that the application logic considered already "used and done with," extending the practical exposure window for secrets well beyond their intended, momentary use.
stepsToIdentify: Use the application to process representative sensitive data (log in, decrypt a protected value, perform a transaction requiring a key).

Immediately after the operation completes (well past when the value should logically still be needed), take a memory snapshot/dump of the running process and search it for the plaintext sensitive value.
Repeat after progressively longer delays to characterize how long the value persists in memory before being overwritten/garbage-collected naturally.

Identify, via decompilation, whether the code uses an immutable string type for the sensitive value (a strong indicator this finding applies) versus a mutable byte buffer that's explicitly zeroed after use.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes process-memory inspection of the test installation.
Trigger the application to process representative sensitive test data.
Capture a memory dump of the running process shortly after the operation completes.
Search the dump for the plaintext sensitive value using a string-search or memory-forensics tool.
Document how long after logical "use" the value remained recoverable, and whether the code's use of an immutable string type versus a properly-zeroed buffer explains the persistence.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

variants: Encryption keys persisting in memory well after the encryption/decryption operation completes, distinct from password/token persistence.
Sensitive data recoverable from a hibernation file or page file (swapped-out memory) even after the process itself has exited, extending exposure beyond the process's own runtime.
Named pipe/IPC interception with weak ACLs allowing lower-privilege access
Memory scraping from accessible process dumps using volatility/WinDbg
mitigation: Use mutable, explicitly-zeroable byte buffers (e.g. `SecureString` where genuinely still appropriate for the platform, or a custom pinned byte array) for sensitive values instead of standard immutable string types, and zero them immediately after use.
Minimize the lifetime and number of copies of any sensitive value in memory — avoid unnecessary string concatenation/manipulation that creates additional, uncontrolled copies.
Where the platform supports it, use OS-level protected-memory APIs (e.g. Windows CryptProtectMemory) for particularly sensitive material like encryption keys.
Disable or encrypt the system page/swap file and hibernation file on machines handling particularly sensitive data, as a compensating control against memory contents being written to disk.

THICK-028.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) capable of modifying the update-check response and serving a substitute package, and a benign proof-of-concept executable to serve as the malicious "update."
THICK-028.whatItIs: The app's auto-updater downloads and runs update files without properly verifying a real cryptographic signature — or checks something so weak (like a simple checksum an attacker can also just recalculate to match their own fake file) that it doesn't actually prove anything. Anyone who can influence the update process — by sitting in the middle of the network connection or compromising the download server — can deliver their own malicious file and have it run with the same trust and privilege as a real update.
THICK-028.rootCause: The updater was built to just download and run whatever file it finds at the expected location, without an independent check that only the real vendor (holding a private signing key the attacker doesn't have) could have produced. A checksum alone doesn't prove anything — if someone swaps the file, they can just as easily recompute a matching checksum for their fake one.
THICK-028.impact: Complete compromise of any machine running the vulnerable auto-updater: an attacker able to intercept or redirect the update channel can deliver arbitrary code that executes with whatever privilege level the update process runs at (often elevated, since installing updates commonly requires administrative rights), representing one of the most severe possible findings in the thick-client domain given the update mechanism's inherent trust and reach.
stepsToIdentify: Capture the application's update-check and package-download traffic via a proxy to identify the exact request/response flow and whether it occurs over TLS.
Determine what integrity mechanism (if any) is applied to the downloaded package: a cryptographic signature verified against an embedded public key, a simple checksum, or no verification at all.
If only a checksum is used, confirm it's genuinely insufficient by substituting an alternate file and recomputing a matching checksum, then checking whether the client accepts it.
If a signature check exists, assess its robustness (does it verify against a properly pinned, non-user-writable public key, or could the trust anchor itself be tampered with locally).
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes update-channel interception and substitute-package delivery testing against the test installation.
Prepare a benign proof-of-concept executable (a harmless action such as writing a test file or popping a message box) to serve as the substitute "update."

Intercept the update-check/download flow via the proxy and substitute the benign proof-of-concept in place of the legitimate package, adjusting any checksum field in the response to match if that's the only check present.
Trigger the client's update installation process and confirm whether the substituted package executes.
Document the exact integrity-verification gap (none, checksum-only, or a bypassable signature check) and the resulting privilege level the substituted code executed at.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

variants: No integrity check at all versus a checksum-only check that provides the illusion of protection without any real cryptographic guarantee.
Signature check present but the embedded/trusted public key or CA is itself stored in a user-writable location, allowing local tampering with the trust anchor even without a network MITM position.
Named pipe/IPC interception with weak ACLs allowing lower-privilege access
Memory scraping from accessible process dumps using volatility/WinDbg
mitigation: Sign all update packages with a private key held exclusively by the vendor, and verify that signature client-side against a public key embedded in (and not independently modifiable within) the application.
Serve updates exclusively over TLS with certificate pinning, in addition to package-level signature verification, as defense in depth against both channel-level and package-level tampering.

Ensure the trust anchor (embedded public key/certificate) cannot be overwritten by a standard local user, since a locally-tamperable trust anchor undermines even a correctly-implemented signature check.

Treat the update mechanism as the single highest-value target in the entire thick-client attack surface during design review, given its inherent broad reach and typically elevated execution privilege.

THICK-029.prerequisites: An installed Electron, NW.js, Tauri or similar web-hybrid desktop application. Ability to unpack the application archive (the app.asar bundle in Electron's case) and read its JavaScript. Access to the app's developer tools where enabled, or a means of injecting content into any window it renders. Authorisation covering local binary modification, since testing involves unpacking and potentially repacking application resources.
THICK-029.whatItIs: An Electron-style application is a bundled web app running in a stripped-down browser, but with one decisive difference: its JavaScript may be granted access to the operating system — filesystem, process spawning, native modules. Whether it is depends on three settings per window: whether Node integration is enabled, whether context isolation is on, and whether the sandbox is enabled. If a window renders any content an attacker can influence while Node integration is on and isolation is off, a cross-site scripting flaw stops being a browser-scoped bug and becomes command execution on the host.
THICK-029.rootCause: Node integration exists because it makes development straightforward — the UI code can simply call filesystem and process APIs directly. Disabling it and routing privileged operations through a narrow, explicitly-defined preload bridge is more work, so applications frequently ship with the permissive configuration retained from early development. Compounding this, developers apply browser-era assumptions about XSS severity to a context where the browser's sandbox has been deliberately removed, and the risk is judged as if it were an ordinary web page.
THICK-029.impact: Any content injection in a Node-enabled window yields arbitrary code execution with the logged-in user's privileges — reading and writing files, spawning processes, establishing persistence, and reaching internal network resources from a trusted endpoint. The injection source need not be exotic: a chat message, a rendered document, a fetched remote page, or a crafted deep link is enough. Because the application is a signed, trusted desktop binary, the resulting activity is attributed to it rather than to obviously malicious software, and endpoint controls frequently permit it on that basis.
stepsToIdentify: Unpack the application bundle and locate the main process source, which is where each window's security options are set.
For every window the app creates, record whether nodeIntegration is enabled, contextIsolation is disabled, and sandbox is off — the dangerous combination is Node on with isolation off.
Inspect any preload script for functions exposed to the renderer, since an over-broad bridge reintroduces the same risk even when Node integration is correctly disabled.
Determine whether the app loads any remote content, renders user-supplied HTML or Markdown, or opens links in an app window rather than the system browser — each is a candidate injection point.
Check whether a Content-Security-Policy is applied to app windows, and whether webSecurity has been explicitly disabled anywhere.
Check the registered custom protocol handlers, since deep links are a common way to reach app functionality from outside and are frequently parsed without validation.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers local binary unpacking and code execution on the test host, and work on a snapshot-capable VM you can restore.
Prove the configuration first by reading the window options directly from the unpacked source — this establishes the finding without executing anything.
Where an injection point is confirmed, demonstrate reach with a benign, clearly-marked action such as writing a distinctly named file to a temporary directory.
Do not escalate to a full payload; showing that the Node API is reachable from renderer context is sufficient to establish severity.
Where a preload bridge is present, enumerate exactly which functions it exposes and test whether any accepts a path or command argument without validation.
Report the specific window and its exact option set, since the fix is a per-window configuration change rather than a general hardening exercise, and remove any test artefacts afterwards.

examplePayloads.label: Benign reachability proof from renderer context

variants: Preload-bridge abuse where Node integration is correctly disabled but the exposed bridge passes attacker-controlled arguments into a privileged operation.
Deep-link injection where a custom protocol handler parses an attacker-supplied URL and routes it into an app window without validation.
Outdated framework version carrying a known renderer escape, which defeats an otherwise-correct configuration.
Disabled webSecurity on a window, permitting cross-origin reads that reintroduce a class of attack the browser would normally prevent.
mitigation: Disable nodeIntegration and enable contextIsolation and sandbox on every window — this is the single change that reduces a renderer compromise back to browser scope.
Expose privileged operations only through a narrow, explicitly-defined preload bridge with validated arguments, never a general-purpose passthrough.
Apply a strict Content-Security-Policy to app windows and never disable webSecurity.
Open external links in the system browser rather than an application window, so remote content never renders in a privileged context.
Validate deep-link input as untrusted, exactly as a web application would treat a request parameter.
Keep the framework version current, since renderer escapes are patched upstream and an outdated runtime undermines correct configuration.
